No. Take P=2, Q=9. The Jacobi symbol is
(92​)=(32​)2=(−1)2=1,
(1)
but the squares modulo 3 are 0,1. A square root of 2 modulo 9 would reduce to one modulo 3, which is impossible. A Jacobi symbol of 1 records a product of local signs; it does not assert that every local sign is positive, or that a quadratic congruence is soluble.

Factor Q=∏i​pi​ and Q′=∏j​qj​, retaining repeated prime factors. If P has a common prime factor with QQ′, it has one with at least one of Q,Q′, and both sides of the desired equality are zero. Otherwise the definition of the Jacobi symbol gives
(QQ′P​)=i∏​(pi​P​)j∏​(qj​P​)=(QP​)(Q′P​).​
(2)
An empty product is 1, so the argument includes either denominator being 1.

For a prime number p, multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol says (PP′/p)=(P/p)(P′/p), including the case of a zero factor. Therefore, writing Q=∏i​pi​ with repetitions,
(QPP′​)=i∏​(pi​PP′​)=i∏​(pi​P​)i∏​(pi​P′​)=(QP​)(QP′​).​
(3)
This product definition still agrees with the stipulated zero when the numerator and denominator are not coprime. For Q=1 all three symbols are 1.

(QP​)=(QP′​).​

The supplementary law for the Legendre symbol is (−1/p)=(−1)(p−1)/2 for odd prime numbers p. For odd integers a,b,
2ab−1​=2a−1​+2b−1​+2(a−1)(b−1)​,
(5)
and the last term is even. Induction over the prime factors of Q therefore gives ∑i​(pi​−1)/2≡(Q−1)/2(mod2). Consequently
(Q−1​)=i∏​(−1)(pi​−1)/2=(−1)(Q−1)/2.​
(6)
For Q=1 the exponent is zero.

The second supplementary law for the Legendre symbol is (2/p)=(−1)(p2−1)/8. To multiply these signs, observe that for odd a,b,
8a2b2−1​−8a2−1​−8b2−1​=8(a2−1)(b2−1)​.
(7)
Both factors in the numerator are divisible by 8, so the right side is even. Applying this identity repeatedly to the prime factorization gives
(Q2​)=i∏​(−1)(pi2​−1)/8=(−1)(Q2−1)/8.​
(8)
Again the convention at Q=1 agrees.

Write P=∏i​pi​, Q=∏j​qj​, counting repetitions. Since P,Q are coprime, every pair pi​,qj​ consists of distinct odd prime numbers. Quadratic reciprocity for the Legendre symbol gives
(qj​pi​​)=(−1)((pi​−1)/2)((qj​−1)/2)(pi​qj​​).
(9)
Multiplying over all i,j and using multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol yields the sign exponent
(∑i​2pi​−1​)(∑j​2qj​−1​)≡2P−1​2Q−1​(mod2),
(10)
by the odd-product parity identity proved in (b)(i). Thus the Jacobi reciprocity law is
(QP​)=(−1)(P−1)(Q−1)/4(PQ​).​
(11)
If either integer is 1, its factorization is empty and both sides equal 1.

Complete the square to obtain the equivalent quadratic congruence
(x+3)2≡1111(mod8093).
(12)
Here gcd(1111,8093)=1: the Euclidean algorithm has successive nonzero remainders 316,163,153,10,3,1. If this modular congruence had a solution, the Jacobi symbol (1111/8093) would be 1, since a square coprime to an odd modulus has Legendre symbol 1 at every prime factor. Calculate instead, using Jacobi reciprocity and reduction of numerators,
(80931111​)​=(11118093​)=(1111316​)=(11114​)(111179​)=(111179​)=−(791111​)=−(795​)=−(579​)=−(54​)=−1.​​(8093≡1(mod4))(8093=7⋅1111+316)(79≡1111≡3(mod4))(1111=14⋅79+5)​
(13)
Therefore there is no solution. This obstruction does not require a separate primality test for 8093; the Jacobi symbol suffices.

2 (Group theory)

2021 OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 134 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 134
a OurBigBook.com
Let ∣G∣=p2. The allowed center of a group theorem gives ∣Z(G)∣>1. By Lagrange's theorem its order is p or p2. In the first case G/Z(G) has order p and is a cyclic group. A cyclic quotient by the center forces G to be Abelian: if G/Z(G)=⟨gZ(G)⟩, write arbitrary elements as gaz,gbw with z,w∈Z(G), and commute them directly. Hence in every case
∣G∣=p2 ⟹ G is abelian.​
(14)
For two examples at prime-cube order, take the dihedral group of a square, ⟨r,s∣r4=s2=1, srs=r−1⟩, and the quaternion group Q8​={±1,±i,±j,±k}. Both have order 8=23. They are nonabelian because sr=rs and ij=k=−k=ji, respectively. They are distinct examples even up to group isomorphism: the dihedral group has five elements of order two and the quaternion group has only one. The request asks for two examples; it does not require the prime to be arbitrary.

Words: 97
b OurBigBook.com
Write ∣G∣=pq with p<q. The Sylow theorems give nq​∣p and nq​≡1(modq). Since p<q, necessarily nq​=1. Its unique Sylow subgroup N is a normal subgroup and has prime order q, so
N≅Cq​⊴G.​
(15)
A Sylow subgroup H≅Cp​ has trivial intersection with N, and ∣NH∣=∣N∣∣H∣=pq, so NH=G. Thus
G≅Cq​⋊Cp​.​
(16)
The semidirect product action is a group homomorphism Cp​→Aut(Cq​)≅Cq−1​. If the action is trivial, G≅Cpq​ by the Chinese remainder theorem; if it is nontrivial, p∣q−1. In particular G has both a cyclic normal subgroup and a cyclic quotient, making it a metacyclic group and hence a solvable group.

Solution

Words: 112
c OurBigBook.com
The Abelian group criterion for a product of two prime squares applies because 11<19 and 11∤192−1=360. Here its Sylow theorems proof is especially short:
n19​∣121,n19​≡1(mod19);n11​∣361,n11​≡1(mod11).
(17)
The candidates for n19​ are 1,11,121, of which only 1 has the required remainder. The candidates for n11​ are 1,19,361, again leaving only 1. Thus both Sylow subgroups P,Q are normal subgroups. Their group commutators lie in P∩Q={1}, and PQ=G, so G≅P×Q. Both factors are abelian groups of prime-square order by (a).
The Fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups gives precisely
C121​×C361​,C121​×C19​×C19​,C11​×C11​×C361​,C11​×C11​×C19​×C19​.​​
(18)
These four groups are pairwise nonisomorphic: their characteristic Sylow subgroups differ in whether they contain an element of order 112 or 192. The first is also the cyclic group C43681​.

d OurBigBook.com
Apply the Abelian group criterion for a product of two prime squares with the smaller and larger primes in their correct order. For p<11, all such groups are Abelian exactly when p∤112−1=120. Of the primes 2,3,5,7, only 7 qualifies. For p>11, the criterion is 11∤p2−1, equivalently p≡±1(mod11). Therefore the exact answer is
p=7orp>11 prime with p≡1,10(mod11).​
(19)
Equivalently, among the stipulated primes p=11, exclude 2,3,5 and the residue classes ±1 modulo 11.
For completeness, the necessity in that criterion supplies actual counterexamples at every excluded prime. If ℓ<q and ℓ∣q2−1, the multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic, so choose α∈Fq2×​ of order ℓ. Let a generator of Cℓ2​ act on the additive group of Fq2​ by multiplication by α. This defines a nontrivial group action, hence a nonabelian semidirect product of order ℓ2q2. Use (ℓ,q)=(p,11) for p=2,3,5, and (ℓ,q)=(11,p) for p≡±1(mod11) with p>11. Thus no excluded prime can be restored to the answer.

35=243≡1(mod121),3≡1(mod121).

A projective transformation of P(Fn+1) is induced by an invertible linear map A:Fn+1→Fn+1:
τ([v])=[Av],A∈GLn+1​(F).​
(22)
This is well defined because replacing v by a nonzero scalar multiple does not change [Av]. Multiplying A by a nonzero scalar also leaves τ unchanged. Conversely these are precisely the transformations in the projective linear group PGLn+1​(F). No field automorphism is included in this definition.

ii

Words: 134 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 134
ii OurBigBook.com
Choose nonzero vectors pi​∈F2 representing Pi​, and write [u,v]=det(u,v). Use the cross-ratio convention
(P0​P1​:P2​P3​)=[p0​,p3​][p1​,p2​][p0​,p2​][p1​,p3​]​.​
(23)
Distinctness makes the denominator nonzero. Every rescaling of a representative occurs once in numerator and denominator, so the value depends only on the projective points. Swapping both pairs simply exchanges the numerator's factors and the denominator's factors:
(P1​P0​:P3​P2​)=[p1​,p2​][p0​,p3​][p1​,p3​][p0​,p2​]​=(P0​P1​:P2​P3​).
(24)
Under an invertible linear map A, [Au,Av]=det(A)[u,v]. Two factors of det(A) occur above and below the fraction, proving projective transformation invariance.
Finally choose homogeneous coordinates making P0​=[1:0], P1​=[0:1], P2​=[1:1]. This normalization exists by the allowed theorem about a projective frame. A point distinct from P0​ is uniquely [t:1], and the displayed cross-ratio is t. Thus equality of the two cross-ratios forces equal coordinates and
P3​=Q.​
(25)
This also shows that for fixed first three distinct points the fourth point is determined by its cross-ratio.

Conjugate by a projective transformation sending P to [1:0] and Q to [0:1]. A matrix representing the conjugated transformation must have zero diagonal, since its first column represents [0:1] and its second represents [1:0]. Therefore it has the form
A=(0b​a0​),ab=0.
(26)
Its square is abI, a nonzero scalar matrix, which induces the identity on the projective line. Conjugating back proves
τ2=id.​
(27)
For the requested explicit involution, take
τ([x:y])=[y:x].​
(28)
More generally [x:y]↦[ay:bx] works whenever ab=0.

i OurBigBook.com
The four points form a projective frame: no three are collinear. By the allowed uniqueness theorem and cross-ratio invariance, use
P0​=[1:0:0],P1​=[0:1:0],P2​=[0:0:1],P3​=[1:1:1].
(29)
Intersecting the indicated projective lines gives
Q0​=[1:0:1],Q1​=[1:1:0],Q2​=[0:1:1].
(30)
A point of Q0​Q2​ has coordinates [a:b:a+b]. Intersecting with P0​P1​, whose equation is z=0, gives Q3​=[1:−1:0]. On that line use its first two homogeneous coordinates. The cross-ratio from (a)(ii) is
(P0​P1​:Q3​Q1​)=(1)(−1)(−1)(−1)​=−1.​
(31)
The characteristic of a field being zero ensures that Q3​=Q1​. The construction is the diagonal-point property of a complete quadrangle, producing harmonic conjugate points.

ii OurBigBook.com
Choose a point A off L, then a point B on AR2​ distinct from A,R2​. Put
P0​=R0​,P1​=R1​,P2​=A,P3​=B.
(32)
These four points form a projective frame: A,B lie off L, and AB=AR2​ meets L at neither R0​ nor R1​. Form, using only joins and intersections,
U=R0​A∩R1​B,V=R0​B∩R1​A,R3​=UV∩L.​
(33)
Here the point called Q1​ in (i) is R2​, while Q3​ is R3​. Thus (i) gives (R0​R1​:R3​R2​)=−1. Interchanging the last two arguments reciprocates the cross-ratio, so
(R0​R1​:R2​R3​)=(−1)−1=−1.​
(34)
All auxiliary choices are possible over a field of characteristic zero, which is infinite. Uniqueness from (a)(ii) shows that the final point is independent of those choices. The picture uses an affine chart in which every relevant intersection is finite; parallel-line exceptions in another chart are ordinary intersections on the projective line at infinity.

(37)
It is a bijection onto R2, with inverse (u,v)↦(3u​,v). Nevertheless DF(s,t)​=diag(3s2,1) is singular whenever s=0. b OurBigBook.com
Fix x∈U. Since U is open, choose an open ball B(x,ε)⊂U. For any y in this ball the segment x+t(y−x) remains in it. For each coordinate Gj​, the chain rule gives
dtd​Gj​(x+t(y−x))=DGj​x+t(y−x)​(y−x)=0.
(38)
The ordinary mean value theorem therefore gives Gj​(y)=Gj​(x) for every coordinate, hence G(y)=G(x). Thus G is a locally constant function.
For each z∈Rm, its preimage is a union of such open balls, so G−1({z}) is open in Rn. Its complement in U is the union of the other fibers and is also open. If U is nonempty and connected, the nonempty fiber through any chosen point is both open and closed in U, and must be all of U. Therefore
DG≡0⟹G locally constant, and constant on connected U.​
(39)
The empty-domain case is vacuous. Notice that continuity of DG was never needed.

DFx​=(a−b​ba​),detDFx​=a2+b2.

DFx​ is invertible exactly when (∂1​f1​(x),∂2​f1​(x))=(0,0).​

ii

Words: 115 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 115
ii OurBigBook.com
Suppose DFx​ were invertible at some x∈Ω. The inverse function theorem supplies a neighborhood V of x for which F(V) is a nonempty open subset of R2. But F(V)⊂M, and a one-dimensional embedded submanifold of R2 has empty interior. To see this last assertion, a slice chart for an embedded submanifold takes M locally into a coordinate line; a coordinate line cannot contain an open plane neighborhood, and a chart preserves openness. This is a contradiction.
Thus DFx​ is singular everywhere. Part (c)(i) strengthens singularity to DFx​=0 everywhere. By (b) and connectedness of Ω,
F is constant.​
(42)
The special form of the Jacobian matrix is essential: an arbitrary differentiable map can have nonconstant image in a curve with derivative of rank one.

Exactly ∣a∣>1 works. Composition with the hyperbolic tangent is smooth for every a. If ∣a∣>1, set R=arctanh(1/∣a∣). For ∣x∣≥R, ∣atanhx∣≥1, so the result vanishes; it is therefore a test function with support of a function [−R,R].
If ∣a∣≤1, every finite x satisfies ∣atanhx∣<1. The given positivity makes ϕ(∣a∣tanhx)>0 for every x, so its support is all of R. In particular ∣a∣=1 is excluded even though the function tends to zero at infinity: decay is not compact support.

For a finite connected graph, a spanning tree contains every graph vertex and is connected and acyclic. A minimum spanning tree minimizes ∑e∈E(T)​w(e) over all such trees. A shortest-path tree rooted at v is a spanning tree whose unique v-to-u graph path has length dG​(v,u) for every graph vertex u. Here the weighted path length is the sum of its edge weights. The two optimizations generally differ, as (b) shows. Connectedness is needed for either spanning-tree object to exist.
For the grid, Kruskal's algorithm examines edges in nondecreasing order of weight and accepts an edge exactly when it joins two different components of the current forest. The weights are encountered in the order
1, 23​, 2, 25​, 3, 27​,….
(70)
The horizontal and vertical acceptance rules are detailed in the two numbered subanswers. Together they produce
E(T)=​{(x,y)(x+1,y):1≤x<n, 1≤y≤n, x≥y−1}∪{(x,y)(x,y+1):1≤x≤n, 1≤y<n, y≥x}.​​
(71)
There are (n−1)(n+2)/2 horizontal and n(n−1)/2 vertical edges, totaling n2−1. Every accepted edge attaches a previously isolated graph vertex to the component already built, so the result is connected and acyclic. The correctness theorem for Kruskal's algorithm, which follows from the minimum spanning tree cut property, proves minimality. Its total cost is
w(T)=[6n(n+1)(n+2)​−1]+12n(n−1)(2n+5)​=12(n−1)(4n2+13n+12)​.​
(72)
For n=1 the tree has one graph vertex, no edges and cost zero. The source's numbered items specify the two edge types; the following subanswers record their contributions to the algorithm.

At weight y the edges considered are precisely the horizontal edges in row y. For y=1 all n graph vertices in that row are isolated, so all n−1 edges are accepted. For y≥2, the first y−1 graph vertices in that row already belong to the one component built by earlier stages, because vertical columns 1,…,y−1 have already been processed. The other graph vertices are isolated. Thus the edges with x<y−1 would create a graph cycle, and all the edges with x≥y−1 are accepted, successively attaching the remaining graph vertices. The rule is
(x,y)(x+1,y) is accepted exactly when x≥y−1.​

By (i), two simple graph paths with different edge sets have different lengths. In particular two distinct simple graph paths from the fixed root v to the same graph vertex u have different edge sets, so there is a unique shortest graph path from v to each u. Positive weights ensure that a shortest walk has no repeated graph vertex: removing a graph cycle strictly reduces its length.
For each u=v, take the final edge of its unique shortest graph path. Every initial segment of a shortest graph path is itself shortest, since replacing it by a shorter one would shorten the whole route. Thus these edges agree with the graph paths' unique predecessors. Following a predecessor strictly decreases dG​(v,u), so no predecessor graph cycle is possible, and all graph vertices eventually connect to v. They form a shortest-path tree. Every other such tree would have to use the same unique root-to-vertex graph paths, proving
the shortest-path tree rooted at v is unique.​
(82)
Literal wording qualification. “Any two paths” needs a convention. Reversing an undirected graph path preserves its edge set and length; distinct zero-edge graph paths at different graph vertices also have length zero. Thus the unrestricted statement is false if these count as different graph paths. The proved edge-set assertion, and in particular uniqueness for graph paths with the same ordered endpoints, is exactly what is needed for the deduction. Arbitrary walks are not included.

By the domination inequality in (i), it follows more strongly that
w(PT​(a,b))<w(e).​

Therefore

TMST​=Tshortest,v​.​

fX​(N∗,N∗)=1,fY​(N∗,N∗)=−(1+b(N∗)2)22rb(N∗)2​=−r2s(r−s)​.
(109)
The first-order Taylor expansion with Nt​=N∗+nt​ therefore gives
nt+1​−nt​+ant−1​=0,a=r2s(r−s)​=r2(r−(δ+1))(δ+1)​.​
(110)
Equivalently, the linearization on (nt​,nt−1​) has matrix (11​−a0​) and characteristic polynomial μ2−μ+a.

For r>s, a>0. When 0<a≤1/4, the roots of μ2−μ+a are real and lie strictly between zero and one. When a>1/4, they are a complex-conjugate pair of modulus a​. Thus the positive steady state is linearly asymptotically stable exactly when 0<a<1, and unstable when a>1. Since a=2s−2s2/r increases strictly with r, the crossing occurs at
a=1,rc​=2s−12s2​=2δ+12(δ+1)2​.​
(111)
At the crossing,
μ±​=21±i3​​=e±iπ/3,nt​=Acos(πt/3)+Bsin(πt/3).​
(112)
Every nonzero real linearized perturbation has period six. This establishes the intended linear stability threshold and linearized period six.
The nonlinear period-six claim in the printed paper does not follow, and is false as a local bifurcating-branch claim for this map. One can check this directly rather than infer a nonlinear period from the eigenvalues. At r=rc​ normalize Nt​=N∗(1+u), Nt−1​=N∗(1+v). The exact planar map is
F(u,v)=((1+u)[2s−1+(1+v)22s2​−(s−1)]−1, u).
(113)
Its cubic Taylor expansion is
F(u,v)=(u−v−uv+2s2−s​v2+2s2−s​uv2+s2s−1​v3, u)+O(∥(u,v)∥4).
(114)
Here is a concrete check of the sixfold return. Put z=(u,v)T, Q=u2−uv+v2, and
K=(12​−2−1​),K2=−3I,α=−s23s2−3s+1​,β=−2s25s2−6s+2​.
(115)
Composing the displayed cubic expansion six times cancels all quadratic terms and gives
F6(z)−z=Q(αI+βK)z+O(∥z∥4).
(116)
In particular
Q(F6(z))−Q(z)=−s22(3s2−3s+1)​Q(z)2+O(∥z∥5).​
(117)
The quartic coefficient is strictly negative. Hence, sufficiently near the equilibrium, every nonzero point has smaller Q after six iterations: the critical nonlinear map has no nearby nontrivial period-six orbit, and the equilibrium itself is locally attracting despite its neutral linearization.
One can also rule out a branch of small period-six orbits on either side of the crossing. Normalize about the positive equilibrium at each nearby r, and put η=a−1. The derivative of the sixth power of (11​−a0​) at a=1 is 3I+K. Smooth dependence on r therefore gives
Fη6​(z)−z=[(3η+αQ)I+(η+βQ)K]z+o((∣η∣+∥z∥2)∥z∥).
(118)
The leading matrix has determinant (3η+αQ)2+3(η+βQ)2. Both terms could vanish with Q>0 only if α=3β, but
α−3β=2s2(3s−2)2​>0.
(119)
Thus its norm on nonzero z is bounded below by a positive constant times (∣η∣+∥z∥2)∥z∥, and the smaller remainder cannot cancel it. There is no nearby nonzero solution of Fη6​(z)=z. The eigenvalues satisfy the nonresonance conditions through order four, their moduli cross outward with increasing r, and the cubic radial coefficient is negative. The standard Neimark–Sacker bifurcation theorem therefore gives a supercritical invariant closed curve. Its rotation is near the linear resonance 1/6; it is not a local branch of exact period-six orbits.
Finally, the discrete population map does not preserve nonnegativity for arbitrary large lagged populations: r/(1+bNt−12​)−δ can be negative. The positive-equilibrium stability conclusions above are local and do not assume a global positivity property that the formula lacks.
